title: Renounce, and enjoy
hookLine: a king says his city can burn and nothing of his will burn
last: ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.

cards: Janaka was the name, or title, of the kings of Mithila; you've met the family before, on day ten and in the Ramayana. The Mahabharata remembers one King Janaka for a single line.
He had palaces, cattle, gold and a kingdom to run, and he said, in plain words: my wealth has no end, because nothing is mine. If Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.
A king, sitting on everything, saying none of it is his. Not a monk who has walked away. A ruler, still ruling.
The second half of the Isha's first verse explains how he could say it.

teach.b: Here's the second half. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: by that renounced, enjoy. Tyakta is let go, given up.
Bhunjitha is enjoy, eat, have the use of. They sit side by side, and that's the surprise. Then a warning, ma gridhah, do not covet, and a question: kasya svid dhanam?

teach.h: DO NOT COVET. WHOSE IS WEALTH?
teach.b: Whose, really, is wealth? The verse has already answered: the Lord's. This is the Hindu idea of tyaga, renunciation, and it isn't only for monks.
Some do leave everything, and they're honored for it. But Janaka stayed king.
His letting go was inside: he stopped owning, and kept using, ruling and enjoying, like a trustee, not a proprietor. Some teachers, Gandhi among them, read the verse exactly that way.
You can watch the teaching happen in a Hindu kitchen. Many families offer food to God before anyone eats: a plate set before the shrine, a few words, a pause. The food is given away first.
Then it comes back as prasad, a gift, and everyone eats it gladly.
Renounce, then enjoy. Nobody goes hungry; the meal just stops being something to grab. It works the same with the things that matter most.
Hold them as lent, and you can enjoy them with both hands. Grip them as only yours, and you spend the meal guarding the plate.

how: Many Hindu families offer food to God before eating and then share it as prasad; some teachers read 'tena tyaktena bhunjitha' in that shape: give it up first, then enjoy it as a gift.

o: by what is let go, given up
by what is earned through work
by what is held tight and kept

games.q: the second half of verse one — tap the pairs.
p: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns

s: the verse says renounce so that you won't enjoy
it says enjoy by renouncing: tena tyaktena bhunjitha.
Janaka gave up his kingdom so he could renounce
he stayed king; his letting go was inside.
the verse ends with a question
kasya svid dhanam: whose, indeed, is wealth?

games.q: nani sets a plate in front of krishna before anyone eats, then everyone shares it. what teaching is that?
o: the food is wasted on a statue.
give it up first, then enjoy it as prasad: renounce, and enjoy.
only the priest may eat it afterwards.
games.why: tena tyaktena bhunjitha: by that renounced, enjoy. the offered plate comes back as a gift.

practice: Before your next drink or meal, pause and offer it, the way many Hindus do. If you pray, say silently, this is yours, or a name of God you love.
Then take the first sip or bite as prasad, something given back to you, and notice whether it tastes any different when it isn't simply yours. If you don't pray, just pause, and receive it as a gift.

wordCard.voice: Tyaktena, by what is let go. Tena tyaktena bhunjitha: by that renounced, enjoy. Don't covet. Whose is wealth?

orig.note: Sanskrit: tyaktena, by what is let go; from tyaj, to give up, the root of tyaga, renunciation.

carryVoice: Your line: renounce it, then enjoy it. Janaka let go of owning and kept the kingdom. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 1 (tena tyaktena bhunjitha, ma gridhah kasya svid dhanam)
Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Janaka: 'if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns')
